questions.question: The modern sandwich is named after which English aristocrat?
questions.fun_fact: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich, allegedly asked for meat between two slices of bread in 1762 so he could keep playing cards without greasy fingers.

questions.question: Which country is widely credited with inventing the croissant?
questions.fun_fact: The croissant descends from the Austrian 'kipferl'. It only became 'French' after Viennese baker August Zang opened a bakery in Paris in 1839.

questions.question: Which two countries officially dispute the invention of French fries?
questions.fun_fact: Belgians claim fries were invented in the Meuse Valley in the 1600s. The 'French' label likely comes from US soldiers in WWI who heard French-speaking Belgians.

questions.question: Hawaiian pizza was actually invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Greek-Canadian Sam Panopoulos invented Hawaiian pizza in Chatham, Ontario in 1962. The name comes from the brand of canned pineapple he used.

questions.question: General Tso's chicken, a staple of American Chinese menus, originated in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Chef Peng Chang-kuei created it in Taiwan in the 1950s. It was sweetened and battered for American tastes when it reached New York in the 1970s.

questions.question: Tikka masala, often called Britain's national dish, was likely invented in which city?
questions.fun_fact: The dish is widely attributed to Glasgow chef Ali Ahmed Aslam in the 1970s, who reportedly added tomato soup and cream to a customer's 'too dry' chicken tikka.

questions.question: Although associated with Chinese restaurants in the West, fortune cookies actually originated in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Fortune cookies trace back to 19th-century Japanese 'tsujiura senbei'. They became associated with Chinese restaurants in California in the early 1900s.

questions.question: Vindaloo, a famously fiery Indian curry, has its name rooted in which European language?
questions.fun_fact: Vindaloo comes from the Portuguese 'carne de vinha d'alhos' (meat in wine and garlic), brought to Goa by Portuguese colonisers.

questions.question: Spaghetti Bolognese, as served abroad, is barely recognised in which Italian city?
questions.fun_fact: In Bologna, ragù is traditionally served with tagliatelle, not spaghetti. The mayor once asked foreign restaurants to stop calling it 'spaghetti bolognese'.

questions.question: The chimichanga, a deep-fried burrito, was reportedly invented in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Legend credits Monica Flin of El Charro Café in Tucson, Arizona (1922), who accidentally dropped a burrito into a deep fryer and exclaimed a Spanish swear word she cleaned up to 'chimichanga'.

questions.question: Which active ingredient was originally in Coca-Cola in the late 1800s?
questions.fun_fact: Coca-Cola contained small amounts of cocaine from coca leaf extract until around 1903. Today it still uses 'decocainised' coca leaf extract for flavour.

questions.question: Under EU law, sparkling wine can only be called 'Champagne' if it comes from which region?
questions.fun_fact: The protected designation of origin restricts the name 'Champagne' to sparkling wine produced in the Champagne region using specific grape varieties and methods.

questions.question: Kopi luwak coffee is famous (and expensive) because the beans are first processed by what?
questions.fun_fact: Asian palm civets eat the coffee cherries, and the beans are collected from their droppings. Enzymes in their gut alter the beans' flavour.

questions.question: Pu-erh tea is unusual because it is intentionally what?
questions.fun_fact: Pu-erh from Yunnan, China, is microbially fermented and can age for decades. Vintage cakes can sell for thousands of dollars per kilogram.

questions.question: Real absinthe gets its green colour primarily from what?
questions.fun_fact: Traditional absinthe's green hue comes from chlorophyll in the final steeping with herbs like hyssop and petite wormwood. The colour naturally fades to amber over time.

questions.question: Gin gets its dominant flavour from which botanical?
questions.fun_fact: By legal definition in the EU and US, a spirit cannot be called gin unless juniper is the predominant flavour.

questions.question: Tequila can only legally be called tequila if it's made from which plant?
questions.fun_fact: Tequila must be made from at least 51% Blue Weber agave and produced in specific regions of Mexico, primarily Jalisco.

questions.question: Butter tea, a staple in Tibet, is typically made with butter from which animal?
questions.fun_fact: Tibetan po cha mixes tea with yak butter and salt. It's drunk all day to combat dehydration and chapped lips at high altitudes.

questions.question: Root beer originally got its distinctive flavour from the root of which plant, later banned by the FDA?
questions.fun_fact: Sassafras root contains safrole, a compound the FDA banned as a food additive in 1960 over cancer concerns. Modern root beer uses safrole-free flavourings.

questions.question: The Maillard reaction, responsible for browning seared meat and toast, is a reaction between what?
questions.fun_fact: Named after French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, it's distinct from caramelisation (which is only sugars) and creates hundreds of flavour compounds.

questions.question: Why does garlic sometimes turn blue or green when pickled or cooked with acid?

answers.text: Sulphur compounds react with amino acids
It absorbs copper from the pot

questions.fun_fact: Garlic's allicin reacts with amino acids to form harmless pigments called pyrroles. The garlic is still safe to eat.

questions.question: 'Sous vide' literally translates from French as what?
questions.fun_fact: Food is sealed in a vacuum bag and cooked in a precisely controlled water bath, allowing very even, consistent cooking impossible with traditional methods.

questions.question: The cooking term 'al dente' literally means what in Italian?
questions.fun_fact: It describes pasta cooked so it still has a slight firmness when bitten — a texture preferred for both flavour and a lower glycaemic response.

questions.question: Adding salt to water for boiling raises the boiling point by roughly how much for normal cooking amounts?
questions.fun_fact: You'd need to dissolve enormous amounts of salt to meaningfully raise the boiling point. We salt pasta water for flavour, not for faster cooking.

questions.question: What is 'mise en place' in a professional kitchen?

answers.text: Everything prepped and in its place before cooking

questions.fun_fact: French for 'putting in place', it's the discipline of pre-measuring, chopping, and arranging every ingredient so service runs smoothly.

questions.question: Why does cutting onions make you cry?

answers.text: They release a volatile sulphur gas that becomes sulphuric acid in your eyes
Onion juice has a high pH

questions.fun_fact: Crushed onion cells release syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a gas that reacts with the water in your eyes to form a mild sulphuric acid, triggering tears.

questions.question: What happens to an egg's white that makes it firm when cooked?
questions.fun_fact: Heat unfolds the egg's proteins, which then tangle and bond into a solid network — a permanent change called denaturation.

questions.question: 'Confit' traditionally refers to food preserved how?

answers.text: Slowly cooked and stored in its own fat

questions.fun_fact: Confit de canard (duck confit) is a Gascon classic — duck legs cured in salt, then slow-cooked and submerged in their own fat, where they keep for months.

questions.question: Why do chefs rest meat after cooking?

answers.text: It lets muscle fibres relax and reabsorb juices
It lowers the internal temperature for safety

questions.fun_fact: While cooking, juices are pushed toward the centre. Resting redistributes them so they don't all run out when you cut in.

questions.question: Carrots were historically what colour before orange ones were popularised?
questions.fun_fact: Wild carrots were purple, yellow, and white. Orange carrots were cultivated by Dutch growers around the 16th–17th century.

questions.question: Botanically speaking, a banana is classified as a what?
questions.fun_fact: Bananas develop from a single ovary with seeds embedded in the flesh, fitting the botanical definition of a berry. Strawberries, ironically, are not berries.

questions.question: Honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs was reportedly still edible because honey does what?
questions.fun_fact: Honey's low water content, low pH, and natural hydrogen peroxide make it inhospitable to microbes. Sealed properly, it can last thousands of years.

questions.question: Why is chocolate toxic to dogs but not to humans?

answers.text: Dogs are allergic to cocoa butter

questions.fun_fact: Humans metabolise theobromine in hours. Dogs take far longer, letting it build to toxic levels that affect the heart and nervous system.

questions.question: Peanuts are botanically not nuts. What are they?
questions.fun_fact: Peanuts grow underground in pods, like peas and lentils. True nuts, like hazelnuts, grow on trees with a hard shell that doesn't open on its own.

questions.question: Cashews are sold shelled because the shell contains what?

answers.text: An irritant chemical related to poison ivy

questions.fun_fact: Cashew shells contain urushiol, the same skin irritant in poison ivy. Workers handle them carefully, and the nuts are roasted to neutralise residue.

questions.question: Apple seeds contain a compound that releases what in the body when chewed?
questions.fun_fact: Apple seeds contain amygdalin, which releases small amounts of cyanide when chewed. You'd need to eat the seeds from dozens of apples for a harmful dose.

questions.question: Most commercial 'wasabi' served outside Japan is actually made primarily from what?
questions.fun_fact: Real wasabi rhizome is hard to grow and expensive. Most paste worldwide is dyed horseradish with a touch of mustard.

questions.question: Lobsters were historically considered such poor food that in colonial America they were fed mainly to whom?
questions.fun_fact: Lobsters washed up by the thousand and were seen as 'sea cockroaches'. Servants in Massachusetts reportedly had clauses limiting how often they could be fed lobster.

questions.question: Most ground cinnamon sold in North America and Europe is not 'true' cinnamon but which cheaper variety?
questions.fun_fact: Cassia is bolder and cheaper but contains more coumarin, which can be harmful to the liver in very large doses. True 'Ceylon' cinnamon has much less.

questions.question: The Michelin star rating system was originally created to do what?
questions.fun_fact: The Michelin tyre company started the guide in 1900 to encourage motorists to drive more — and wear out more tyres — by giving them places to visit.

questions.question: Which country opened a chain of fake McDonald's-style restaurants, including one called 'Mash Donald's'?
questions.fun_fact: With McDonald's absent from Iran, copycat chains using altered logos and names like 'Mash Donald's' and 'Pizza Hat' have popped up in Tehran.

questions.question: Sushi in pre-modern Japan was originally a method primarily designed to do what?
questions.fun_fact: Early 'narezushi' wrapped fish in fermenting rice for months. The rice was thrown away, and only the preserved fish was eaten. Modern nigiri came later, in Edo Japan.

questions.question: In Japan, slurping noodles loudly at a ramen shop is generally considered what?
questions.fun_fact: Slurping cools noodles, aerates the broth, and signals enjoyment. It's the opposite of Western table manners.

questions.question: What is unusual about how 'fugu' (pufferfish) chefs in Japan are licensed?

answers.text: They train for years to remove organs containing a deadly toxin
They must be born in a coastal prefecture
They can only serve it under government supervision

questions.fun_fact: Pufferfish liver and ovaries contain tetrodotoxin, far deadlier than cyanide. Chefs train for years and must pass a strict exam before they can prepare and serve fugu.

questions.question: In South Korea, what 'dining' activity has become a massive online entertainment genre?

answers.text: Mukbang — eating huge meals on camera

questions.fun_fact: Mukbang ('eating broadcast') hosts livestream themselves eating enormous portions, often earning a living from viewer donations and ads.

questions.question: What is the traditional purpose of tipping the bill in many parts of Japan?

answers.text: There isn't one — tipping is generally not done
To skip the queue next time

questions.fun_fact: In Japan, good service is the standard, not a bonus. Tipping can be seen as awkward or even rude; staff may chase you down to return the money.

questions.question: In Italy, ordering a cappuccino after about 11 a.m. is widely considered what?

answers.text: A foreigner move — locals usually drink it only in the morning

questions.fun_fact: Italians believe milky coffee interferes with digestion after meals, so cappuccino is breakfast-only. Espresso or macchiato is the post-meal norm.

questions.question: In a French restaurant, what does it traditionally mean if you place your knife and fork parallel on your plate?
questions.fun_fact: Crossed cutlery means 'I'm still eating'. Parallel placement, usually at the 4 o'clock position, tells the server they can clear your plate.

questions.question: The world's oldest restaurant still in operation, according to Guinness, is in which city?
questions.fun_fact: Sobrino de Botín in Madrid has been serving roast suckling pig from its wood-fired oven since 1725. The oven has reportedly never been allowed to go out.

questions.question: Tomatoes, central to Italian cuisine, were originally brought to Europe from where?
questions.fun_fact: Tomatoes arrived in Europe via Spanish conquistadors in the 16th century. For about 200 years, many Europeans grew them only as ornamentals, fearing they were poisonous.

questions.question: Forks took centuries to be accepted in Europe partly because the Catholic Church considered them what?
questions.fun_fact: When a Byzantine princess introduced the fork to Venice in the 11th century, clergy condemned it as an affront to God, who gave us natural forks — our fingers. It took until the 18th century to become standard at European tables.

questions.question: Margarine was originally invented in the 1860s in response to a contest sponsored by which ruler?
questions.fun_fact: Napoleon III offered a prize for a cheap butter substitute to feed the army and the poor. Chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès won in 1869 with a beef-fat product he called oleomargarine.

questions.question: The potato was treated with such suspicion in 18th-century France that one promoter posted armed guards around a potato field for what reason?

answers.text: To make peasants think the crop was valuable and worth stealing
To stop foreign spies from copying the variety
Because potatoes were taxed at gold-equivalent rates

questions.fun_fact: Antoine-Augustin Parmentier deliberately had his royal potato plots guarded by day and left unguarded at night. Locals duly stole the 'precious' tubers and planted them in their own gardens.

questions.question: Ketchup originally referred to a sauce based on what — long before tomatoes were involved?
questions.fun_fact: The word likely comes from a Hokkien Chinese fermented-fish sauce called 'kê-tsiap'. British sailors copied it with mushrooms and walnuts, and tomato versions only appeared in the early 19th century in America.

questions.question: When you whip cream, what physically traps the air to make it fluffy?
questions.fun_fact: Whisking partially destabilises the fat in cream so the globules clump around air bubbles, holding them in place. Skim milk has too little fat to whip — that's why only high-fat cream works.

questions.question: Bread rises because yeast produces what gas as it digests sugars?
questions.fun_fact: Yeast also produces alcohol as a by-product, but most of it evaporates during baking. The CO2 is what gets trapped in the gluten network and makes dough expand.

questions.question: Why does pineapple sting your tongue when eaten raw?

answers.text: An enzyme called bromelain digests proteins in your mouth
Its citric acid level is unusually high
Tiny calcium crystals scratch the tissue

questions.fun_fact: Bromelain literally starts breaking down the proteins on your tongue's surface. Cooking or canning destroys the enzyme, which is why canned pineapple doesn't sting.

questions.question: Adding a tiny amount of which compound to scrambled eggs causes them to set with a noticeably greener tint?

answers.text: Iron, often from cast-iron cookware reacting with sulphur

questions.fun_fact: When egg sulphur reacts with iron, it forms iron sulphide — a greenish-grey compound. The same reaction is why overcooked hard-boiled yolks develop a green ring around them.

questions.question: Hot peppers feel hot because capsaicin binds to which receptor in your mouth?

answers.text: A bitterness receptor on the tongue
A pressure receptor under the gums

questions.fun_fact: Capsaicin tricks the same receptor that would fire if you actually touched something hot. That's why your brain reacts with sweating and a rushing pulse even though nothing is burning.

questions.question: Why is milk fat from grass-fed cows often yellower than fat from grain-fed cows?

answers.text: Beta-carotene from fresh grass colours the fat
Higher iron levels in the blood
Sun exposure on the animal's hide

questions.fun_fact: Cows pass beta-carotene from fresh forage into their milk fat. Many industrial butters in winter add carrot or annatto colouring so blocks look consistent year-round.

questions.question: Why does adding a pinch of salt to a slice of melon often make it taste sweeter?

answers.text: Salt suppresses bitterness so the sweetness comes through more clearly
Salt chemically converts starch into sugar on the surface
Sodium directly activates sweet taste buds

questions.fun_fact: Sodium ions block some bitter taste signals. With less bitterness in the way, the brain perceives the same sugars as a stronger sweet flavour — the same trick is used in salted caramel and chocolate.

questions.question: Ceviche, a famous raw-fish dish, is most closely associated with which country?
questions.fun_fact: Ceviche is Peru's national dish — fish 'cooked' chemically by the citric acid in lime juice. The leftover marinade, called leche de tigre ('tiger's milk'), is drunk as a hangover cure.

questions.question: Hákarl, a traditional Icelandic delicacy, is made from what?
questions.fun_fact: Greenland shark meat is toxic when fresh because it's full of urea. Icelanders bury it for weeks to ferment, then hang it to cure for months. The result smells strongly of ammonia.

questions.question: Poutine, smothering fries in gravy and cheese curds, originated in which Canadian province?
questions.fun_fact: Multiple Quebec diners claim the invention in the 1950s. The fresh squeaky curds are essential — older curds melt and ruin the texture.

questions.question: The Ethiopian staple injera is a spongy flatbread made primarily from which grain?
questions.fun_fact: Teff is a tiny grain native to the Ethiopian highlands. Injera batter is fermented for days before being cooked, giving it a tangy, slightly sour flavour and characteristic bubbly surface.

questions.question: Casu marzu, a banned-in-most-of-the-EU Sardinian cheese, is intentionally infested with what?
questions.fun_fact: Producers leave pecorino cheeses open so the cheese fly Piophila casei lays eggs in them. The maggots break down the fats, producing a creamy, intensely pungent paste eaten with the larvae still wriggling.

questions.question: Pad thai, today seen as a quintessential Thai dish, was actually promoted by the government in the 1930s–40s for what reason?

answers.text: To build a national identity and reduce rice consumption
To use surplus shrimp from the navy

questions.fun_fact: Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram pushed pad thai as part of a nation-building campaign. Replacing pure rice meals with rice-noodle dishes saved rice for export during wartime.

questions.question: By volume, what is the single largest ingredient in beer?
questions.fun_fact: Beer is typically over 90% water. That's why brewing cities like Pilsen or Burton-on-Trent built their reputations on the mineral content of their local water as much as on the malt.

questions.question: Bavaria's Reinheitsgebot of 1516 originally restricted beer to only which three ingredients?
questions.fun_fact: Yeast wasn't on the original list because brewers didn't yet understand it — they thought fermentation just 'happened'. Yeast was added centuries later once Pasteur demonstrated its role.

questions.question: A 'flight' on a tasting menu refers to what?

answers.text: A small set of related drinks tasted side by side
A dessert course served between savoury dishes
An aged spirit served in a stemmed glass

questions.fun_fact: Beer, wine, and whisky flights typically come in three to five small pours, arranged from light to heavy so each one is judged before palate fatigue sets in.

questions.question: Sparkling wine made in the same method as Champagne, but outside that region, undergoes its second fermentation where?

answers.text: In an open vat under pressure
In a steel pressure tank only

questions.fun_fact: The 'méthode traditionnelle' traps the CO2 from the second fermentation inside each bottle. Cheaper sparkling wines like Prosecco use the simpler Charmat method, fermenting in big tanks.

questions.question: Decaffeinated coffee is not fully caffeine-free; a typical cup still contains roughly what?

answers.text: About half the caffeine of regular coffee

questions.fun_fact: Most decaf processes remove around 97% of the caffeine, leaving a few milligrams per cup. Several cups can add up to the same dose as a single espresso.

questions.question: Black, green, oolong, and white teas all come from the leaves of which single plant species?
questions.fun_fact: The differences come from how the leaves are processed — mostly how much they're oxidised. Herbal 'teas' like rooibos or chamomile aren't true tea at all, just infusions.

questions.question: Single malt Scotch whisky must, by law, be made from a mash of what?

answers.text: Only malted barley, at a single distillery
A blend of barley, corn, and rye
Any grain, as long as the whisky is aged 12+ years

questions.fun_fact: 'Single' refers to a single distillery, not a single cask. The mash must be 100% malted barley and the whisky must be matured in oak casks in Scotland for at least three years.

questions.question: Bourbon, by US federal regulation, must be made from a grain mix containing at least how much corn?
questions.fun_fact: Bourbon must also be aged in new, charred oak barrels. The charring caramelises sugars in the wood and is what gives bourbon its golden colour and vanilla notes.

questions.question: A 'three Michelin star' rating, in the guide's own wording, means a restaurant is what?
questions.fun_fact: One star is 'a very good restaurant', two is 'worth a detour', three is 'worth a special journey'. The wording dates back to when the guide was telling motorists how far to drive.

questions.question: In Italy, the small extra charge added to a restaurant bill simply for sitting down is called what?
questions.fun_fact: Coperto literally means 'cover'. It originally paid for bread and the table linen, and it's usually a euro or two per person — separate from any service charge.

questions.question: A traditional French restaurant 'brigade' is the kitchen hierarchy formalised by which famous chef?
questions.fun_fact: Escoffier borrowed military structure to break the chaotic kitchens of his day into clear stations: saucier, poissonnier, pâtissier and so on. Most modern restaurants still echo his system.

questions.question: What does it mean when a restaurant kitchen calls 'fire' on a dish?

answers.text: Start cooking it now so it lands with the rest of the order
Discard it because it's been sitting too long
The chef is officially refusing the dish

questions.fun_fact: Orders are usually called in two steps: 'ordering' tells the line a ticket is in, and 'fire' tells them to actually start cooking it so all components hit the pass together.

questions.question: Vanilla, the world's second-most-expensive spice, comes from the cured pods of which plant?
questions.fun_fact: The orchid is native to Mexico, where it was pollinated by a specific stingless bee. Outside that range, every flower has to be hand-pollinated, which is why real vanilla is so expensive.

questions.question: Saffron threads, sold by weight at gold-like prices, are which part of the crocus flower?
questions.fun_fact: Each crocus has only three stigmas, and they must be hand-picked. It takes roughly 150,000 flowers to produce a single kilogram of dried saffron.

questions.question: Black, white, and green peppercorns all come from the same plant. What is the main difference between them?

answers.text: When they're harvested and how they're processed
They come from male versus female vines
Different soils used in their cultivation

questions.fun_fact: Green is unripe; black is unripe and dried with the skin on; white is ripe with the skin removed. Pink 'peppercorns' aren't actually pepper at all — they come from an unrelated tree.

questions.question: Cloves, the small dark spice common in mulled wine, are actually what part of a plant?
questions.fun_fact: Cloves are buds from a Southeast Asian evergreen tree, picked before they open and then sun-dried. Their main active compound, eugenol, is so strong it's used in dentistry as a mild anaesthetic.

questions.question: Sourdough bread rises without commercial yeast because it relies on what?

answers.text: Wild yeast and bacteria from a starter culture
The bread's own gluten expanding under heat

questions.fun_fact: A sourdough starter is a living mix of wild yeasts and lactobacilli. The bacteria produce lactic and acetic acids, which is what gives sourdough its tang and improves keeping quality.

questions.question: An authentic French baguette is, by tradition, made from only how many ingredients?

answers.text: Four — flour, water, salt, and yeast
Two — sourdough starter and water only

questions.fun_fact: A French decree from 1993 defines the 'baguette de tradition' and forbids any additives. The shape standardised in the 20th century partly because long, thin loaves bake faster.

questions.question: Pita bread puffs up into a hollow pocket because of what?

answers.text: Steam trapped between two thin layers of dough
Air whipped into the dough before baking

questions.fun_fact: Very hot ovens flash the moisture in the thin dough into steam, blowing the top and bottom apart. When the bread cools and deflates, the gap stays — perfect for stuffing.

questions.question: Pumpernickel, the dense dark German bread, gets much of its colour from which slow cooking process?

answers.text: Burning off the crust in an open flame
Mixing molasses directly into the dough

questions.fun_fact: Traditional pumpernickel bakes at low temperatures for up to 24 hours. The long, gentle heat triggers Maillard reactions that deepen the bread to nearly black without burning it.

questions.question: Chocolate was consumed for most of its history not as a bar but as what?
questions.fun_fact: The Maya and Aztecs drank cacao mixed with chilli, vanilla, and sometimes maize, often frothed by pouring between vessels. Solid eating chocolate only appeared in the 19th century.

questions.question: The first solid milk chocolate bar was developed in 1875 in which country?
questions.fun_fact: Daniel Peter combined cocoa with the powdered milk that his neighbour Henri Nestlé had recently invented. The pair effectively created the milk-chocolate industry that Switzerland is still famous for.

questions.question: Modern sweet ice cream became practical in the 19th century mainly thanks to which invention?

answers.text: The hand-cranked freezer with ice and salt

questions.fun_fact: Nancy Johnson's 1843 patent for a hand-cranked ice-cream maker used a salt-and-ice bath around an inner can. The endothermic mix dropped temperatures below freezing long before household electric freezers existed.

questions.question: Marshmallows were originally made from the sap of which plant, used as a sore-throat remedy?
questions.fun_fact: Ancient Egyptians whipped marsh-mallow root sap with honey for royalty. Modern marshmallows replaced the plant extract with gelatine in the 19th century, keeping only the name.

questions.question: On New Year's Eve in Spain, tradition calls for eating exactly twelve of what as the clock strikes midnight?
questions.fun_fact: Eating one grape per chime is said to bring good luck for each month of the coming year. The tradition is often credited to Alicante grape growers marketing a 1909 surplus.

questions.question: In South Korea, what dish is traditionally eaten on one's birthday for good luck and long life?
questions.fun_fact: Mothers eat miyeokguk after giving birth for its iron and iodine, and children eat it on every birthday in remembrance. Skipping it on your birthday is considered a missed tradition.

questions.question: Many Japanese families have come to associate Christmas Eve dinner with which Western fast-food brand, thanks to a 1970s ad campaign?
questions.fun_fact: KFC's 'Kentucky for Christmas' campaign launched in 1974 and stuck. Today many Japanese families pre-order their Christmas KFC bucket weeks in advance, and stores have long queues on December 24.

questions.question: The blue veins in cheeses like Roquefort and Stilton come from what?

answers.text: Penicillium mould introduced into the cheese
Bruising of the curds when pressed

questions.fun_fact: Cheesemakers pierce the wheels with needles or wires so air reaches the inside, letting the introduced Penicillium roqueforti or P. glaucum grow and develop those blue-green veins.

questions.question: Authentic Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese must be aged for at least how long before it can be sold under that name?
questions.fun_fact: Inspectors tap each wheel with a hammer and listen for flaws before approving it. Wheels are graded; only the best can be aged further and stamped as longer-aged Parmigiano-Reggiano.

questions.question: Mozzarella di bufala, the prized Italian mozzarella, is made from the milk of what animal?
questions.fun_fact: Water buffalo milk has roughly twice the fat of cow milk, giving the cheese its rich, creamy interior. The protected version must come from specific regions of southern Italy.

questions.question: Soy sauce, miso, and sake all owe their flavour to the same Japanese mould known as what?
questions.fun_fact: Koji breaks starches into sugars and proteins into amino acids, building deep umami flavour. Japan designated A. oryzae its 'national fungus' in 2006 in recognition of its cultural importance.

questions.question: Sauerkraut and kimchi are both preserved primarily by which kind of fermentation?
questions.fun_fact: Lactobacillus species on the raw cabbage thrive in the salty, oxygen-poor brine and turn sugars into lactic acid. The acid both preserves the vegetables and gives them their characteristic tang.

questions.question: Kombucha is brewed by fermenting sweet tea with a culture commonly nicknamed what?
questions.fun_fact: SCOBY stands for 'symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast'. The rubbery disc floats on the tea, with the yeast producing alcohol and the bacteria converting it into the drink's tart acids.

questions.question: Why does popcorn pop?

answers.text: Water inside the kernel turns to steam and bursts the hull
The sugars caramelise and expand suddenly
Trapped air pockets heat up and crack the shell

questions.fun_fact: A popcorn kernel needs about 14% moisture sealed inside its hard hull. The trapped water flashes to steam at high pressure, and when the hull finally gives way, the starchy inside explodes and turns inside out. Too-dry kernels won't pop at all.

questions.question: Why does bread go stale even when it's kept perfectly sealed and moist?

answers.text: The starch molecules recrystallise, a process called retrogradation
The bread slowly dries out no matter how it's stored
Mould begins growing invisibly inside the crumb

questions.fun_fact: Staling isn't really about losing water — it's the starch reorganising into a firmer crystal structure as it cools. That's why warming stale bread briefly makes it soft again: the heat reverses the retrogradation for a while.

questions.question: Why does a freshly poured glass of cola eventually go flat?

answers.text: Dissolved carbon dioxide escapes back into the air
The sugar absorbs the bubbles over time
The acid neutralises and stops producing gas

questions.fun_fact: Soda is bottled under pressure to force extra CO2 into the liquid. Once opened, the gas is no longer held in and slowly diffuses out. Rough surfaces and scratches give bubbles a place to form, which is why a poured glass goes flat faster than the sealed bottle.

questions.question: Why does adding a little acid like lemon juice help keep cut apples from browning?

answers.text: It slows the enzyme that reacts with oxygen
It seals the surface with a sugar coating
It kills bacteria that cause the colour change

questions.fun_fact: Cut fruit browns because an enzyme reacts with oxygen to form brown pigments. Acid lowers the pH below the level that enzyme needs to work, and the vitamin C in citrus also mops up oxygen, so the flesh stays pale longer.

questions.question: Why does a cup of coffee or tea look darker in the middle and lighter at the thin edge?

answers.text: Less liquid depth means less colour for light to pass through
The surface oils concentrate toward the centre
Heat rising from the middle changes the colour

questions.fun_fact: The colour you see depends on how much liquid the light travels through. At the shallow rim there's barely any depth, so more light gets through and it looks paler — the same reason a deep sea looks darker than a shallow puddle of the same water.

questions.question: Why does whisking egg whites turn them from clear liquid into a stiff white foam?

answers.text: Beating unfolds the proteins so they trap air and bond together
The whisking adds tiny ice crystals that hold the shape
Friction heat partly cooks the whites

questions.fun_fact: Egg white is mostly water and tightly coiled proteins. Whisking physically unwinds those proteins, which then link up around the air bubbles, building a stable scaffold. A trace of fat or yolk wrecks it, because fat interferes with the protein bonds.

questions.question: Why does sparkling wine famously go 'pop' and shoot the cork when uncorked?

answers.text: Pressure inside the bottle is several times atmospheric pressure
The cork expands and snaps free as it warms
Shaking creates a small chemical explosion

questions.fun_fact: A Champagne bottle holds roughly three times the pressure of a car tyre, created by trapped CO2 from the second fermentation. The thick glass and wired cork exist to contain it — released suddenly, a cork can leave the bottle at highway speeds.

questions.question: Why does butter, but not olive oil, turn solid in the fridge?

answers.text: Butter's fats are mostly saturated and pack tightly when cold
Olive oil has a natural antifreeze compound

questions.fun_fact: Saturated fats are straight molecules that stack neatly into a solid at cool temperatures. Olive oil is rich in unsaturated fats with kinked shapes that can't pack together easily, so it stays liquid in the fridge — though it will eventually cloud and thicken if cold enough.

questions.question: Why do you smell food more strongly when it's hot than when it's cold?

answers.text: Heat makes the aroma molecules evaporate faster into the air
Hot food produces brand-new scent chemicals
Heat opens up the nostrils to take in more air

questions.fun_fact: Smell relies on volatile molecules reaching receptors in your nose, and heat gives them the energy to lift off into the air. It's why warm bread is intensely fragrant and why ice cream needs a lot of sugar and fat to taste rich — cold dulls both aroma and sweetness.

questions.question: Why does milk sometimes curdle when you pour it into hot coffee or tea?

answers.text: Acidity and heat make the milk proteins clump together
The caffeine chemically splits the milk fat
Tannins freeze the proteins on contact

questions.fun_fact: Milk proteins stay dispersed at neutral pH, but coffee and tea are mildly acidic, and heat speeds the reaction. Older milk is already slightly more acidic as it sours, so it curdles far more readily even before it tastes off.

questions.question: Why does freshly baked bread feel soft but a baguette crust goes crackly and hard?

answers.text: The crust loses moisture and the sugars there brown and harden
The crust is made from a different, denser dough
Steam is deliberately kept away from the crust

questions.fun_fact: The outer surface reaches high temperatures, driving off water and triggering browning reactions that leave a brittle, dry shell. Bakers actually inject steam early in baking to delay the crust setting, which lets the loaf expand fully before the surface crisps.

questions.question: Why does a watermelon make a hollow, deep sound when you tap a ripe one?

answers.text: A ripe melon's flesh is looser and resonates at a lower pitch
Ripe melons contain a pocket of gas inside
The rind thins out and vibrates more as it ripens

questions.fun_fact: As a watermelon ripens, the cell walls in the flesh break down and the fruit becomes less dense and springier. That changes how it vibrates when tapped — an unripe melon sounds higher and tighter, a ripe one sounds deeper and more resonant.

questions.question: Why does salt make ice melt and is used to grit roads in winter?

answers.text: Salt lowers the freezing point of water
Salt chemically reacts with ice to produce heat
Salt is darker and absorbs more sunlight

questions.fun_fact: Dissolved salt gets in the way of water molecules trying to lock into ice crystals, so the water must get colder than 0°C before it can freeze. The same principle lets old ice-cream makers reach sub-freezing temperatures using an ice-and-salt bath.

questions.question: Why does honey eventually turn cloudy and grainy in the jar?

answers.text: The sugars crystallise out of the dense syrup
It is starting to ferment and spoil
Water is slowly evaporating from the surface

questions.fun_fact: Honey is a supersaturated sugar solution — it holds more sugar than would normally dissolve. Over time some of that sugar comes out as crystals, especially when cool. It's a sign of purity, not spoilage, and gentle warming dissolves it back to clear liquid.

questions.question: Why does cooking pasta make the water turn cloudy and a bit slippery?

answers.text: Starch leaches out of the pasta into the water
The pasta releases trapped air bubbles
Salt reacts with the flour to form a film

questions.fun_fact: As pasta cooks, surface starch dissolves into the water, making it cloudy. That starchy water is prized by cooks: a splash of it helps a sauce cling to the noodles and emulsify, which is why many recipes say to save a cupful before draining.

questions.question: Why does a carbonated drink fizz up violently when you drop a mint sweet into it?

answers.text: The sweet's rough surface gives countless bubbles a place to form at once
The mint chemically reacts with the cola to make new gas
The sweet dissolves and releases its own trapped air

questions.fun_fact: The classic mint-and-cola geyser is physics, not a chemical reaction. The candy's pitted surface is covered in microscopic nooks, each one a launch site where dissolved CO2 can rapidly form bubbles, releasing the gas almost all at once.

questions.question: Why does meat shrink and tighten on the grill as it cooks?

answers.text: Heat makes the muscle proteins contract and squeeze out water
The fat melts away and leaves the meat smaller
The surface seals and traps everything inside

questions.fun_fact: As proteins heat up they coil tighter and wring moisture out of the meat, which is why an overcooked steak ends up smaller and drier. It's also why a thin patty can curl into a dome — the edges contract faster than the middle.

questions.question: Why does chopping or crushing garlic make it far more pungent than leaving the clove whole?

answers.text: Damage triggers an enzyme reaction that creates the sharp compounds
Cutting releases an oil that was sealed in the centre
Air rushing in oxidises the surface instantly

questions.fun_fact: An intact clove barely smells. Breaking the cells lets an enzyme meet a separate compound, and only then does it form allicin, the molecule behind garlic's bite. Letting crushed garlic rest a few minutes before cooking lets that reaction finish for a stronger flavour.

questions.question: Why does a cold fizzy drink go flat faster when it warms up?

answers.text: Warmer liquid can hold less dissolved gas
Heat speeds up a chemical reaction that destroys the bubbles
The warmth thickens the liquid and traps less gas

questions.fun_fact: Gases dissolve better in cold liquids than warm ones, the opposite of how solids like sugar behave. As a drink warms, it simply can't hold as much CO2, so the gas escapes more quickly — which is why warm soda fizzes over the moment you open it.

questions.question: Why does a microwave heat a bowl of soup but leave the ceramic bowl relatively cool?

answers.text: The microwaves agitate water molecules, and the bowl has little water
The metal in the microwave only heats food, not containers
Ceramic reflects the microwaves back into the food

questions.fun_fact: Microwaves are tuned to make water molecules rotate rapidly, generating heat from within the food. A dry ceramic bowl has almost nothing for the waves to grab, so it only gets warm by contact with the hot soup — which is why the handle of a mug can stay cool while the drink scalds.

questions.question: Why does a pinch of cornstarch or flour thicken a sauce as it heats?

answers.text: The starch granules swell and absorb the liquid
The flour reacts with the fat to form a gel
It lowers the boiling point so the sauce reduces faster

questions.fun_fact: In heat and moisture, starch granules drink up surrounding water and balloon, getting in each other's way and thickening the mix — a process called gelatinisation. Overheat it or add too much acid and the granules burst and the sauce thins back out.

questions.question: Why do leafy vegetables turn a brighter green for a moment when you first drop them in boiling water?

answers.text: Heat drives out tiny gas bubbles that were dulling the colour
Boiling creates new green pigment in the leaves
The water dissolves a brown coating off the surface

questions.fun_fact: Raw leaves have microscopic air pockets between their cells that scatter light and mute the colour. Brief heat collapses that air, so the vivid green of the chlorophyll shows through. Keep cooking, though, and acids break the chlorophyll down to a drab olive.

questions.question: Why does cream become whipped cream but eventually turn into butter if you keep beating it?

answers.text: Over-beating forces the fat globules to clump into solid butter
The air escapes and the cream collapses into fat
Friction heat melts and re-solidifies the cream

questions.fun_fact: Whipping first coats air bubbles with fat to make a foam. Keep going and the fat globules slam together so hard their membranes rupture and they fuse, squeezing out the watery buttermilk and leaving a solid lump of butter — exactly how butter has always been churned.

questions.question: Why does a glass of cold water fog up on the outside on a humid day?

answers.text: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface
Water seeps through tiny pores in the glass
The cold makes the glass sweat out its own moisture

questions.fun_fact: The droplets come from the air, not the drink. When humid air touches the chilled glass it cools below its dew point and can't hold all its moisture, so water condenses on the outside — the same reason a chilled bottle of beer or wine 'sweats' on a warm day.

questions.question: The word 'salary' comes from a Roman practice connected to which seasoning?
questions.fun_fact: 'Salary' derives from the Latin 'salarium', linked to soldiers' pay and salt, which was once so valuable it was used almost like currency. The phrase 'worth his salt' echoes the same idea.

questions.question: The cocktail and the rooster-tail share a name because 'cocktail' is thought to originally describe what?

answers.text: A type of rooster feather garnish

questions.fun_fact: One leading theory traces 'cocktail' to horses whose tails were docked so they stuck up like a rooster's, making them look lively and spirited — a quality then applied to a lively, mixed drink.

questions.question: The Caesar salad is named after a person, not the Roman emperor. Who was he?

answers.text: A Roman general who loved greens
A French chef named Jules César

questions.fun_fact: Italian-American Caesar Cardini reportedly improvised the salad in his Tijuana restaurant in 1924 when a busy Fourth of July left the kitchen low on ingredients. He tossed it tableside to make it a spectacle.

questions.question: The Margherita pizza was supposedly named in 1889 to honour whom?
questions.fun_fact: The pizza's tomato, mozzarella, and basil are said to mirror the red, white, and green of the Italian flag, made for the visiting queen. The story is much-loved even if historians debate its details.

questions.question: Graham crackers were invented in the 1800s by a preacher who intended them to do what?

answers.text: Suppress unhealthy urges and curb the appetite
Replace bread during a wheat shortage

questions.fun_fact: Sylvester Graham promoted a bland, plain diet he believed would calm the passions and discourage vice. His plain whole-wheat cracker was meant to be deliberately unexciting — the opposite of today's sweet, honeyed version.

questions.question: The word 'whisky' comes from a Gaelic phrase meaning what?
questions.fun_fact: 'Whisky' descends from the Gaelic 'uisge beatha', meaning 'water of life' — a direct echo of the Latin 'aqua vitae'. Several European spirits, like aquavit, carry the same hopeful name.

questions.question: Worcestershire sauce was reportedly created by accident when an early batch was what?

answers.text: Forgotten in a cellar and left to age for months
Spilled into a barrel of vinegar
Boiled far too long by mistake

questions.fun_fact: The story goes that chemists Lea and Perrins found their first attempt unpalatable and abandoned the barrels. Rediscovered much later, the fermented sauce had mellowed into something delicious.

questions.question: The pretzel's distinctive knotted shape is traditionally said to represent what?
questions.fun_fact: One legend credits a medieval monk who shaped leftover dough to look like a child's arms crossed in prayer, giving the treats to children who learned their prayers. The three holes were sometimes linked to the Trinity.

questions.question: The English word 'ginger' and the spice's name ultimately trace back to a root word in which ancient language?
questions.fun_fact: The name passed from Sanskrit through Greek and Latin into English over many centuries. The spice itself travelled the same long trade routes from South Asia, which is why so many languages share a similar-sounding word for it.

questions.question: Popsicles were famously invented by an 11-year-old who did what?

answers.text: Left a cup of soda and a stir-stick outside overnight in the cold
Mixed crushed ice with fruit syrup at a fair
Froze juice in a metal ice tray on purpose

questions.fun_fact: Frank Epperson left flavoured soda powder, water, and a stirring stick on a porch in 1905; a freezing night did the rest. He patented the frozen treat as an adult, calling it the 'Epsicle' before it became the Popsicle.

questions.question: Nachos got their name from the nickname of the man who improvised them. What was his job?

answers.text: A restaurant maître d' improvising a snack for guests

questions.fun_fact: Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya reportedly threw together fried tortillas, cheese, and jalapeños for hungry diners in Piedras Negras, Mexico, around 1940 when the kitchen was closed. The dish took his nickname.

questions.question: Tea bags are widely said to have been created by accident when a merchant did what?

answers.text: Sent tea samples in small silk pouches customers brewed whole
Dropped loose tea into a sieve made of cloth
Wrapped tea in paper to keep it dry at sea

questions.fun_fact: Early-1900s New York merchant Thomas Sullivan mailed tea in little silk bags as samples. Customers, unsure what to do, dunked the whole bag in hot water — and liked the convenience so much they asked for more.

questions.question: The word 'restaurant' originally referred to what?

answers.text: A restorative meat broth sold to revive customers
A roadside inn for tired travellers

questions.fun_fact: In 18th-century Paris, a 'restaurant' was a fortifying bouillon meant to 'restore' health. The word later shifted to mean the establishment that served such restoratives, then any eating house.

questions.question: Tonic water originally contained quinine because it was used to fight which disease?
questions.fun_fact: British colonists in tropical regions drank bitter quinine tonic as an anti-malarial, then mixed in gin, sugar, and lime to make it palatable — effectively inventing the gin and tonic as medicine.

questions.question: Pound cake earned its name because the original recipe called for what?

answers.text: A pound each of flour, butter, sugar, and eggs
A cake weighing exactly one pound when baked
Dough that was pounded by hand for an hour

questions.fun_fact: The simple one-pound-of-everything ratio made the recipe easy to remember and pass along by word of mouth in an era when many bakers couldn't read — no written recipe required.

questions.question: The English word 'cappuccino' comes from a comparison to what?

answers.text: The brown hooded robes of Capuchin friars
A small monkey with a frothy mane

questions.fun_fact: The drink's colour was likened to the robes of Capuchin monks. The same monks lent their name to the capuchin monkey, whose colouring also resembles that distinctive hooded brown.

questions.question: The chilli pepper got its confusing 'pepper' name because Columbus believed it was related to what?

answers.text: Black peppercorns he was sent to find

questions.fun_fact: Columbus was searching for the lucrative black-pepper trade of the East Indies. When he met the spicy New World fruit, he called it 'pepper' too — and the misnomer stuck across countless languages.

questions.question: The dessert known as Peach Melba was created by a famous chef in honour of whom?

answers.text: A Australian fruit grower named Melba

questions.fun_fact: Chef Auguste Escoffier created the peach-and-raspberry dessert in the 1890s for soprano Nellie Melba. Melba toast, the thin crisp bread, was also named for her after she was served it during an illness.

questions.question: The word 'barbecue' most likely entered English from which language?

answers.text: A Caribbean Taíno word for a wooden cooking frame
A French phrase meaning 'beard to tail'
A Spanish word for a charcoal pit

questions.fun_fact: It comes from the Taíno 'barbacoa', a raised wooden grate for slow-cooking meat over a fire. The popular 'beard-to-tail' French story is a charming folk etymology with no real evidence behind it.

questions.question: Brandy got its name from a Dutch word describing how it was made. What does that word mean?
questions.fun_fact: 'Brandy' shortens the Dutch 'brandewijn', meaning 'burnt wine' — a nod to distillation, where wine is heated to concentrate the alcohol. Dutch traders spread both the technique and the name across Europe.

questions.question: Carbonated soft drinks exist largely because an 18th-century scientist figured out how to do what?

answers.text: Infuse water with the gas given off by brewing beer
Trap volcanic gas in sealed bottles
Boil mineral springs to release bubbles

questions.fun_fact: Joseph Priestley suspended water above a brewery's fermenting vats to dissolve the carbon dioxide, inventing artificially carbonated water in 1767. He hoped fizzy water might cure scurvy at sea — it didn't, but it launched the soda industry.

questions.question: The English word 'biscuit' literally means what, describing how it was originally made?
questions.fun_fact: From the Latin 'bis coctus', 'biscuit' refers to bread baked twice to dry it out completely. This made it last for months at sea or on campaign — the original purpose of ship's biscuit and hardtack.

questions.question: The bagel's signature boiled-then-baked method exists mainly to give it what?

answers.text: A chewy, dense crust that resists going stale

questions.fun_fact: Briefly boiling the dough sets the outer starch before baking, creating that distinctive shiny, chewy crust. The sturdy result travelled and kept well — practical for the communities that popularised it.

questions.question: Chewing gum as we know it became possible thanks to chicle, a substance originally chewed by which people?
questions.fun_fact: Chicle is the dried sap of the sapodilla tree, chewed in Mesoamerica for centuries. It reached the US in the 1860s via exiled Mexican general Santa Anna, who hoped to sell it as a rubber substitute before it became gum.

questions.question: Roughly how much water does it take to produce a single 250 ml glass of milk, counting the cow's feed and drinking water?
questions.fun_fact: Most of that 'water footprint' goes into growing the grass and feed crops the cow eats, not the water it drinks directly. A single glass of milk hides roughly a bathtub's worth of water.

questions.question: A teaspoon of pure caffeine powder is enough to do what to an adult?

answers.text: Keep them awake for exactly 24 hours
Have no effect, as it's too diluted

questions.fun_fact: A lethal dose is roughly 10 grams, about a teaspoon of the pure powder. You'd need around 75 to 100 cups of coffee to reach that, which is why brewed coffee is safe but the raw powder is regulated.

questions.question: What is the maid pouring into the bowl in this painting?
questions.fun_fact: Vermeer painted the milkmaid around 1660. The bread on the table and the bowl point to a bread pudding — a dish made of leftovers, painted with a blue that cost more than gold at the time.

questions.question: What are the people in this 1885 painting eating?
questions.fun_fact: Van Gogh wanted it visible that the hands digging the earth are the same hands reaching into the dish. His brother Theo thought the picture too dark; Van Gogh long considered it his best.

questions.question: What is stacked on this Dutch still life from 1615?
questions.fun_fact: Stacked cheese was a status symbol in the Dutch Golden Age: it showed trade, wealth and a full larder at once. The tabletop tilts towards the viewer on purpose, so that everything can be seen at the same time.

questions.question: Which animal is lying on the table here?
questions.fun_fact: The lobster was the luxury item of these banquet still lifes — cooked red, expensive, perishable. That is exactly why it is there: the paintings show abundance and remind you it does not keep.

questions.question: Which fruit is cut open in this watercolour?
questions.fun_fact: A pineapple is botanically not one fruit but many small berries fused together. The plate comes from a collection of some 7,500 watercolours the US Department of Agriculture commissioned before colour photography existed.

questions.question: What percentage of a cucumber is water?
questions.fun_fact: 96 percent — more than a watermelon. That is also why it tastes of almost nothing until it is salted.

questions.question: How many litres of milk go into one kilogram of hard cheese?
questions.fun_fact: Around ten — nearer fourteen to sixteen for a long-aged hard cheese such as Parmigiano. The rest drains off as whey, a waste product for centuries and now the expensive powder in sports nutrition.

questions.question: How many months must Parmigiano Reggiano age at minimum?
questions.fun_fact: Twelve, by protected-designation rules, after which an inspector taps every wheel with a small hammer. Fail and the wheel loses its rind branding.

questions.question: At what temperature does table sugar start to caramelise?
questions.fun_fact: Browning starts around 160 °C — before the sugar has properly melted, since pure sucrose melts at about 186 °C. Past that point caramel turns bitter within seconds.

questions.question: How many Scoville units does a jalapeño carry?
questions.fun_fact: About 5,000. A habanero sits near 200,000 and pure capsaicin at 16 million — the scale has no upper bound and was originally judged by tongue.
